steps.label: Constructive methods
steps.speakerNotes: Level: undergraduate (year 3). Made from the lecture lec05-kp05 with view-from-text-v3: pages were planned first and each page is mainly one native infographic (designed in HTML and converted to native nodes), with the terms defined on the same page. 10 pages; every number is computed by program.

steps.label: Master unit
steps.speakerNotes: This is the first page of KP05. Prerequisites: a step unit turns a score into a bit 0 or 1; codes and purity (if two points of different classes have exactly the same code, the output layer cannot separate them); and the four XOR points (0,0 and 1,1 are B, 0,1 and 1,0 are A). The construction of KP04 knew the equation of the target region, but in practice we only have points and labels. This page takes z1 equal to f of x1 plus x2 minus 0.5: (0,0) scores minus 0.5, bit 0; (0,1) and (1,0) score 0.5 and (1,1) scores 1.5, all bit 1. So the 0 group has 1 point and the 1 group has 3 points (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the mixed group.

steps.label: Mixed group
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the master unit's two groups. This page checks the labels group by group. The 0 group holds only (0,0), truth B, called B, right. The three points of the 1 group are all called A: (0,1) and (1,0) are A and right, (1,1) is B and wrong. So 3 points are right and 1 is wrong. A mixed group is an output group containing both classes; here it has 3 points (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the ancillary unit.

steps.label: Ancillary unit
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the mixed group. For the demonstration this page picks one ancillary line by hand: z2 equal to f of 1.5 minus x1 minus x2, and the line x1 plus x2 equal to 1.5 lies between (1,1) and (0,1), (1,0). (0,1) and (1,0) score 0.5 and bit 1; (1,1) scores minus 0.5 and bit 0. (0,0) is not in the mixed group and takes no part in training; its z2 equal to 1 is merely computed on the side. This shows the mechanism and is not the result of running a training algorithm (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the purified codes.

steps.label: Purified codes
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the ancillary unit. This page joins the two bits: (0,0) is 01, (0,1) and (1,0) are 11, and (1,1) is 10. Purification adds bits so points of different classes no longer share exactly the same code. With z1 alone the mixed group has 3 points; with the full code the three groups 01, 11, 10 are all pure, so 0 points are mixed. Purification does not require one code per class: B using both 01 and 10 is fine (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the new code plane.

steps.label: New code plane
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the purified codes. This page looks at the new (z1, z2) plane: the two A merge at 11, B sits at 01 and 10, and 00 has no point. The new master unit takes z1 plus z2 minus 1.5 and calls A above 0: 11 scores 0.5 and is A, 01 and 10 score minus 0.5 and are B. All four points are right; merging the two A at 11 is fine because they are the same class (computed by program). Next, the next page covers why it stops.

steps.label: Why it stops
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the new code plane. This page gives the reason for stopping. Progress one: within a layer the mixed group still to be resolved shrinks strictly, here from 3 points to 0. Progress two: under a suitable construction between layers, the new master unit keeps the points already right and gets at least one more; let Ck be the number of points the layer-k master units get right, then C(k+1) is at least Ck plus 1 and Ck is at most N; here it rises from 3 to 4. This condition is required by the cited construction and is not a general conclusion verified by this example, and this page does not prove it. An integer cannot keep increasing, so it stops. Note that 3 to 0 counts mixed-group points, not an error rate (computed by program). Next, the next page covers the stopping conditions.

steps.label: Stopping conditions
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on why it stops. This page gives the conditions for stopping. First, labels must not contradict: when two identical inputs carry different classes, a deterministic network has only one output for that input, so it cannot be right on both. Second, units must be added by rule for strict progress; adding neurons at random does not guarantee a stop. A common myth says that if the training points end up all right, new data must be right too; all right concerns only the given points and does not guarantee unseen places, nor a minimal network. Generalization is the ability to classify data not seen in training. Next, the next page covers the perpendicular bisector.

steps.label: Bisector line
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the stopping conditions. This page is an extension: another route, nearest neighbour, comparing distances through the perpendicular bisector of two training points. Let u and v be two training points; expanding the equal-distance condition cancels the common quadratic term and gives 2 times (v minus u) transpose x equal to the squared length of v minus the squared length of u. Take u as (0,0) and v as (1,0): 2 x1 equal to 1, that is, x1 equal to 0.5; the point (0.5, 0.7) on the line is 0.860 from both. N points have at most N(N minus 1)/2 pairs: 6, 45 and 4950 for 4, 10 and 100 points; this does not mean all are kept, nor is it a minimal network size. This is only a distance comparison of two points, not a full nearest-neighbour network experiment (computed by program). Next, the next page covers three layers suffice.

steps.label: Three layers suffice
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on the perpendicular bisector. This page separates existence from procedure. After the first layer the inputs are binary codes, and KP04's detectors with an OR-merge classify the purified codes, which shows that a suitable three-layer representation suffices; but the layer-by-layer growing procedure is not guaranteed to stop within three layers. Existence and a depth guarantee for the procedure are not the same theorem. Next, the next page covers the exercises.

steps.label: Exercises
steps.speakerNotes: Following the previous page on three layers suffice. Two exercises. Q1: grouped by the full code, 01 is (0,0), B; 11 is (0,1) and (1,0), A, A; 10 is (1,1), B; all pure, 0 mixed points. With z1 alone 3 points are mixed; 3 to 0 counts the still-mixed points, while the error rate counts wrong points, and the master unit alone gets 1 wrong. Q2: the same input gives the same output, so a deterministic network gives one answer and cannot be right on both A and B (computed by program). That ends this unit; next, move on to the next unit.
